conversation.text: The stone vaulted ceiling gathers the wind into a low, mournful howl. The leaded glass window frames vibrate with the airflow. player6 looks around, a strand of hair pulled to the corner of their mouth by the draft. The Bora wind seeps in through every stone joint.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Is the wind here... always this abnormal?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The nun scrapes wax stains from the candlestick base with her fingernail. It's been like this for three hundred years.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Always like this?" "Hasn't it been more abnormally strong recently?"

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The nun inserts the copper candle spike back into the plaster crack. Not too bad yet. When the wind is strong, the stained glass windows seep ice shards. Nowadays, it just capsizes a few more fishing boats.

"It's like this: my recently deceased mentor mentioned this name in his diary." "My mentor said he had a pleasant conversation with Mr. Winkelmann, and they agreed to exchange papers."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Looking through the railings, a four-story red brick building covered in withered ivy vines, the plaster pediment on the Corinthian colonnade eroded into honeycomb-like holes by the wind. Just then, the brass door knocker clacks, and a young man in a tweed coat squeezes out the door crack holding a stack of books. His tortoiseshell glasses slide down to his reddened nose tip. The edges of the manila folder tucked under his arm are frayed and curled. The wind tousles the light brown curls on his forehead.

conversation.speaker: player3
conversation.text: #Simply look around, intending to visit as a guest. #Beside this person, greet politely. "Hello, sir. I am an archaeology professor from Miskatonic University." "A friend wrote me a letter asking me to visit an acquaintance." "But because my careless friend didn't leave much detail in the letter." "So I'd like to visit the local Dean of Academic Affairs in an academic exchange capacity."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Good day, madam. Scholars from Miskatonic University are always held in high esteem. Which professor specifically is the acquaintance you mentioned? I am Vittorio Caldara, a teaching assistant in the Classical Literature Department, just on my way to deliver these archives to the Academic Affairs Office. If you don't mind, I can take you to see Dean Marino on the way—he should currently be sorting newly acquired Etruscan pottery shards. The young man pushes his slipped glasses back into place, freeing a hand to point at the oak door on the second floor with a brass nameplate.

conversation.speaker: player4
conversation.text: "Ahem, if I recall correctly, it's Mr. Winkelmann."

conversation.speaker: player3
conversation.text: "Yes, that's right." "Winkelmann, Johann Winkelmann."

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Winkelmann? The young man suddenly stops walking, the books swaying slightly in his arms. He frowns, showing a puzzled expression, then pulls a leather-bound Trieste Art History from the top of the stack, quickly flipping to a page with a faded bookmark. On the yellowed paper is a lithograph rubbing: a winged figure reclining on a sarcophagus surface, with Latin inscriptions on the side. Bolan's temple throbs. The first moment she saw Winkelmann in London, she also thought of him, but quickly dismissed it. Winkelmann, the father of modern archaeology. The person you think you'll meet died on June 8, 1768. "The Johann Joachim Winkelmann you mentioned—the founder of modern archaeology—was murdered in this city 155 years ago. The art museum's garden still displays his relics." He closes the book.

conversation.speaker: player1
conversation.text: Prayers received! Continuing to record the howling cold wind—Trieste 1923. Currently recorded text: 543 entries. Time elapsed: 2 hours, 55 minutes, 22 seconds. Huh? A piece of paper flew out when opening the file. Some would call this practice of utterly eliminating intelligent life, preserving only inorganic matter, an evil war crime. We call it efficient.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: Since arriving in Trieste, you have been following Winkelmann's clues. The day after checking in, you head to the local university. At the university's iron gate, you meet Vittorio Caldara, the teaching assistant carrying books. After Bolan states her identity as a Miskatonic professor, player4 mentions seeking Winkelmann, only to learn he was murdered 155 years ago. The assistant closes the art history book, mentioning that the art museum displays the deceased's relics.

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The museum stands at the end of Via della Cattedrale, its gray-white stone walls forming a stark angle with the spire of the Cathedral of San Giusto. Gothic arched windows are fitted with wire mesh. Gargoyles on the cornices noisily spit water into the pool below. The ticket office is a tin booth embedded under the arcade. Behind the glass window sits an elderly man in uniform, a newspaper covering most of his face, gray sideburns peeking from the edge of Il Piccolo.

conversation.speaker: player3

conversation.speaker: player2
conversation.text: The old man slowly lifts his wrinkled face from behind the newspaper, his gray-blue eyes examining you through copper-framed glasses. He folds the newspaper into a neat square with thin fingers. "It's open. Two lire each." He points to a wooden sign nailed beside the window, painted in black: 10:00-16:00. About 67 lire left.

conversation.speaker: player2
